hints: Think what secondary means for the carbon bearing the OH group, it must be joined to two other carbon atoms, so place the OH on an inner carbon of the four carbon chain.
walkthrough:
Picture what secondary tells you**
A secondary alcohol has the $\text{-OH}$ group on a carbon that is attached to two other carbons. For $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ draw a chain of four carbons. If you put $\text{OH}$ on carbon 1 you get a primary alcohol, so move it to carbon 2: $\text{CH}_3\text{-CH(-)-CH}_2\text{-CH}_3$.

Draw every bond out fully**
Displayed means show every atom and every bond. Draw $\text{C-C}$, $\text{C-H}$ and $\text{C-O}$ bonds explicitly, and very importantly draw $\text{O-H}$ as $\text{-O-H}$, not just $\text{-OH}$. That gives $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ fully displayed.
Final answer: Displayed formula of butan-2-ol: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ with all bonds and the $\text{O-H}$ bond shown.

hints: Focus on where the Br ends up, the carbon skeleton is unchanged from S so the Br simply replaces the OH at the same position.
walkthrough:
Track the carbon skeleton**
Step 1 converts $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ to $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Br}$. The four carbon chain of butan-2-ol is unchanged, the $\text{-OH}$ on carbon 2 is just swapped for $\text{-Br}$. Number the longest chain to give the substituent the lowest number, so Br is on carbon 2 of butane, giving 2-bromobutane.

hints: Compare the functional groups before and after step 1, one group leaves and a different single atom takes its place on the same carbon.
walkthrough:
See the swap**
You start with $\text{C-OH}$ in S and finish with $\text{C-Br}$ in T. One group ($\text{OH}$) has been exchanged for another ($\text{Br}$) at the same carbon with no change in carbon chain length. When one atom or group replaces another, that is the definition of substitution.

hints: Look at the change from $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Br}$ to $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{CN}$, identify which nucleophile must supply the $\text{CN}$ group.
Recall why the solvent must be ethanol rather than water for this reaction, to favour substitution over hydrolysis to an alcohol.
walkthrough:
Spot the chain extension by one carbon**
T is $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Br}$ and U is $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{CN}$. The Br is replaced by $\text{CN}$, so you need a source of cyanide ions, $\text{CN}^-$. That is $\text{NaCN}$ or $\text{KCN}$.

Choose conditions that favour substitution**
Cyanide acts as a nucleophile here. Use ethanol as solvent, not water, otherwise you would get the alcohol by hydrolysis. Heat the mixture under reflux to provide energy for the substitution to occur.
Final answer: Reagent: $\text{NaCN}$ or $\text{KCN}$\nConditions: heat under reflux in ethanol / ethanolic and heat

hints: Recall the product of heating a nitrile with dilute acid, the $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$ group is fully hydrolysed to a carboxylic acid group plus an ammonium ion.
Count atoms to balance, you will need two water molecules to supply the two O atoms for the $\text{COOH}$ group.
walkthrough:
Recognise nitrile hydrolysis**
Heating $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{CN}$ (U) with dilute acid adds water across the $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ bond. The organic product is the carboxylic acid $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{COOH}$, which has formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_2$. The nitrogen ends up as $\text{NH}_4^{+}$ in acid.

Balance with acid and water**
Write the full balanced equation: $$\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{CN} + \text{H}^{+} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{NH}_4^{+}$$ Check it: two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ molecules provide the two O atoms needed for $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, and $\text{H}^{+}$ balances the charge to form $\text{NH}_4^{+}$.

hints: Scan the spectrum above $1500 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ and look for a sharp absorption that is absent in alcohols and bromoalkanes, then match it to the Data Booklet value for a triple bond.
walkthrough:
Use the distinctive peak to fingerprint U**
S is an alcohol and would show a broad $\text{O-H}$ absorption around 3200-3600 $\text{cm}^{-1}$, which is not present. T is a bromoalkane with no strong absorption above $1500 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ except $\text{C-H}$. The spectrum shows a sharp medium peak at about 2250 $\text{cm}^{-1}$. That region is characteristic of the $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ triple bond stretch, which only U ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{CN}$) contains. So the sample must be U.
Final answer: Sharp absorption at 2200-2250 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ due to $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ confirms U.
